lead: A stress state at a point is not one number. It is a small table of normal and shear stresses on three faces, and six independent values fix it. Engineers label it uniaxial, biaxial or triaxial to choose the right formula for strength, strain and failure. The geometry and restraints decide whether a problem is plane stress or plane strain; once that choice is made it fixes σ<sub>z</sub> (zero for plane stress, ν(σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>) for elastic plane strain) and every later result.
prereq: You need Unit 1: normal and shear stress, Hooke's law and Poisson's ratio.

sections.h3: Stress at a point: six numbers

blocks.text: Take a tiny cube at a point. On each face there is a normal stress σ and two shear stresses τ. For equilibrium, τ<sub>xy</sub> = τ<sub>yx</sub>, so nine components reduce to six: σ<sub>x</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub>, σ<sub>z</sub>, τ<sub>xy</sub>, τ<sub>yz</sub>, τ<sub>zx</sub>. Tension is positive. The first index of τ<sub>xy</sub> is the face normal; the second is the direction. Some books swap this order.
σ = ( σ<sub>x</sub>  τ<sub>xy</sub>  τ<sub>zx</sub> ; τ<sub>xy</sub>  σ<sub>y</sub>  τ<sub>yz</sub> ; τ<sub>zx</sub>  τ<sub>yz</sub>  σ<sub>z</sub> )
blocks.where: σ is the stress tensor; σ<sub>x</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub>, σ<sub>z</sub> are normal stresses; τ<sub>xy</sub>, τ<sub>yz</sub>, τ<sub>zx</sub> are shear stresses, with τ<sub>xz</sub> = τ<sub>zx</sub>; all in MPa.

blocks.text: The tensor describes the point, not the whole body. A tensile bar has one nonzero normal stress on its cross-section. A shaft in torsion has shear. A beam in bending has normal stress varying across depth (see Unit 4). The six numbers are enough to find stresses on any plane, which is the job of 2.2 and transformation in 2.3.

A uniaxial state has only one nonzero normal stress, often σx; all other normals and shears are zero. A tensile test coupon away from the grips is close to this. A biaxial state has two nonzero normal stresses. A thin cylinder under internal pressure has hoop and longitudinal stresses (Unit 7), a common biaxial field. If the third normal stress is zero and shear on that face is zero, the state is plane stress. Biaxial loading is therefore often treated as a plane-stress problem. Principal axes are in 2.4.

A triaxial state has three nonzero normal stresses. A point deep in a thick cylinder or under a bearing contact is triaxial. Hydrostatic pressure has all three normals equal and compressive; it is triaxial but has no shear. The labels count nonzero principal normal stresses. They do not count the number of lines in a drawing.

sections.h3: Plane stress, plane strain and the spherical split

blocks.text: Plane stress means σ<sub>z</sub> = 0 and τ<sub>xz</sub> = τ<sub>yz</sub> = 0, but ε<sub>z</sub> is not zero. A thin plate loaded in its plane is close to plane stress. Plane strain means ε<sub>z</sub> = 0, not σ<sub>z</sub> = 0. A long dam or a long retaining wall changes little along its length. For an elastic isotropic material, setting ε<sub>z</sub> = 0 gives σ<sub>z</sub> = ν(σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>). With σ<sub>x</sub> = 100 MPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = 40 MPa and ν = 0.3, σ<sub>z</sub> = 42 MPa, not zero.

blocks.where: σ<sub>m</sub> is the mean normal stress in MPa; σ<sub>x</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub>, σ<sub>z</sub> are the three normal stresses in MPa.

blocks.text: The advanced split writes the tensor as a spherical part plus a deviatoric part. The spherical part has σ<sub>m</sub> on all three diagonals and zero shear. The deviatoric part is the original tensor minus the spherical part. The spherical part tends to change volume; the deviatoric part tends to change shape and drives yielding in ductile metals. Only a few universities teach this split in Strength of Materials; it is standard in advanced solid mechanics.

examples.question: At a point in a machine part, the normal stresses are σ<sub>x</sub> = 120 MPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = 60 MPa and σ<sub>z</sub> = 0. All shear stresses are zero. (a) Name the stress state. (b) Split the stress tensor into spherical and deviatoric parts.
steps: Write the tensor. All shear stresses are zero, so only the three diagonal terms remain: σ<sub>x</sub> = 120 MPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = 60 MPa, σ<sub>z</sub> = 0.
Two normal stresses are nonzero and σ<sub>z</sub> = 0 with zero shear on the z-face. The state is biaxial plane stress.
Spherical part: put 60 MPa on all three diagonals. The spherical tensor is diag(60, 60, 60) MPa.
Deviatoric part: subtract the spherical part from the original tensor. The deviatoric tensor is diag(120 − 60, 60 − 60, 0 − 60) = diag(60, 0, −60) MPa.
examples.answer: The state is biaxial plane stress. The mean stress is 60 MPa; the spherical part is diag(60, 60, 60) MPa; the deviatoric part is diag(60, 0, −60) MPa.
examples.check:
sx = 120.0
sy = 60.0
sz = 0.0
mean = (sx + sy + sz) / 3.0
print(mean)
print(mean)
print(mean)
print(mean)
print(sx - mean)
print(sy - mean)
print(sz - mean)

traps: Calling any two-dimensional drawing plane stress when the problem states plane strain. In plane strain, ε<sub>z</sub> = 0, and σ<sub>z</sub> = ν(σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>), not zero.
Mixing biaxial with plane stress. A biaxial state has two nonzero principal normal stresses; a plane-stress state is fixed by σ<sub>z</sub> = 0 and zero shear on the z-face.
Forgetting the mean-stress denominator. The mean uses all three normal stresses, so σ<sub>m</sub> = (σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub> + σ<sub>z</sub>) / 3, not the average of two.
Sign slips in the deviatoric part. Use deviatoric = original − spherical. A compressive normal stress is negative, so its deviatoric value can be positive after subtraction.
Thinking a hydrostatic stress changes shape. Equal normal stresses on all faces give no shear and no distortion; the deviatoric part is the shape-changing part.

quiz.q: Name the six independent stress components at a point and state the unit used for stress in this chapter.
quiz.a: σ<sub>x</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub>, σ<sub>z</sub>, τ<sub>xy</sub>, τ<sub>yz</sub>, τ<sub>zx</sub>. Stress is in MPa.

quiz.q: Why does a stress tensor have six independent components instead of nine?
quiz.a: Moment equilibrium gives τ<sub>xy</sub> = τ<sub>yx</sub>, τ<sub>yz</sub> = τ<sub>zy</sub> and τ<sub>zx</sub> = τ<sub>xz</sub>. Three pairs become equal, so nine components reduce to six.

quiz.q: A point has σ<sub>x</sub> = 100 MPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = 50 MPa, σ<sub>z</sub> = 0 and all shear stresses zero. Name the stress state and find the mean normal stress.
quiz.a: Two normals are nonzero and σ<sub>z</sub> = 0, so it is biaxial plane stress. σ<sub>m</sub> = (100 + 50 + 0) / 3 = 50 MPa.

quiz.q: In plane strain, σ<sub>x</sub> = 100 MPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = 40 MPa and ν = 0.3. Find σ<sub>z</sub>.
quiz.a: For elastic plane strain, σ<sub>z</sub> = ν(σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>) = 0.3 × (100 + 40) = 42 MPa.

quiz.q: A long retaining wall is analysed as plane strain, but a thin plate is analysed as plane stress. Explain the difference in the out-of-plane condition.
quiz.a: Plane strain sets ε<sub>z</sub> = 0 because the long wall cannot stretch along its length; σ<sub>z</sub> is generally nonzero. Plane stress sets σ<sub>z</sub> = 0 because the thin plate has free surfaces; ε<sub>z</sub> is generally nonzero.

quiz.q: A state has σ<sub>x</sub> = σ<sub>y</sub> = σ<sub>z</sub> = −80 MPa and zero shear. Is it uniaxial, biaxial or triaxial? What is its deviatoric part?
quiz.a: All three normals are nonzero, so it is triaxial. The mean is −80 MPa. The deviatoric part is diag(−80 − (−80), −80 − (−80), −80 − (−80)) = diag(0, 0, 0) MPa.

quiz.q: Why is a thin cylinder under internal pressure called a biaxial stress case?
quiz.a: Its wall carries hoop stress and longitudinal stress, both normal stresses in the wall. The radial stress is small through the thin wall, so two normal stresses dominate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Finite element software stores every stress state as a tensor and reports invariants such as mean stress and von Mises stress. Soil mechanics uses triaxial tests to describe failure under three different principal stresses. Metal forming and additive manufacturing track deviatoric stress because shape change and residual stress depend on it. Search for stress tensor invariants, deviatoric stress and plane strain conditions to go deeper.
